452.text: This occurrence matches spoude's usual 'earnestness/zeal' sense as elsewhere in 2 Corinthians (7:11-12; 8:7); no divergence from that pattern appears here.

454.text: Earnest care (G4710), as this word's own vantage: it is the content God places into the heart (G2588), and its presence there is the ground of Paul's thanks (G5485) -- it is the causal center that both the heart's reception and the resulting thanksgiving depend on.

606.text: G4709 and G4710 share the same root and semantic arc; G4710 supplies the same relational-earnestness sense that G4709 exhibits, seen concretely in Luke 1:39 (haste to a kinswoman) and 2Cor 8:16 (earnest care placed in Titus's heart for the Corinthians) -- both members thus converge on urgency/zeal directed toward persons, not only tasks.

608.text: G4710 is exclusively nominal across all twelve of its occurrences (N-ASF, N-GSF, N-DSF forms), meaning the subgroup's noun-member consistently names diligence/zeal/haste as a possessable, giveable, or measurable quality (something one 'shows', 'has produced in you', 'puts into a heart', or is measured 'by') -- structurally opposite to G4709's pure manner-of-action adverbial function. This is the clearest grammatical-role divergence between the two subgroup members: G4710 names the THING, G4709 describes the HOW.

778.text: The characteristic reads as belonging to created design rather than the fallen condition: it is commended as a positive Christian virtue to be exercised (Rom 12:8, 12:11; Heb 6:11; 2Pet 1:5) and modeled even by God himself in placing it in Titus's heart (2Cor 8:16) -- there is no instance where earnestness itself is portrayed as a fallen distortion, only its absence (idleness/sloth) is negatively marked.

782.text: Yes. The mode varies by direction: God-to-person (2Cor 8:16, earnest care put into Titus's heart by God), person-to-person (Luke 7:4 pleading for another; Titus 3:13 provisioning for others; 2Tim 1:17 searching for Paul), and person-toward-God/spiritual-goal (Rom 12:11 zeal in serving the Lord; Heb 6:11 earnestness toward hope; 2Pet 1:5 effort in supplementing faith). It operates at the level of will/action throughout, never at a merely bodily-reflex level.

788.text: Yes. Within existing relational bonds (kinship, close ministry partnership) the characteristic appears as warm, sustained care -- Luke 1:39 (Mary to kinswoman Elizabeth), 2Cor 8:16 (Titus's earnest care for the Corinthians, put there by God), 2Tim 1:17 (Onesiphorus's earnest search for his friend Paul). Across relational distance or unfamiliarity it appears as urgent advocacy or provision on behalf of someone less close -- Luke 7:4 (Jewish elders pleading for a Gentile centurion), Titus 3:13 (provisioning traveling workers). The characteristic thus operates in both settings but with differing textures: relational bonds intensify it into personal devotion, while distance channels it into practical intercession or hospitality.

790.text: The relational scope is broad: it includes fellow believers (2Cor 8:16, Titus's care for Corinthians), ministry partners and traveling workers (Titus 3:13, 2Tim 1:17), kin (Luke 1:39), and even those outside the community of faith or covenant (Luke 7:4, elders for a Gentile centurion). No occurrence shows the characteristic explicitly excluding any category of person; where it is withheld, it is due to personal sloth/idleness rather than the exclusion of a class of people.

794.text: Where God himself is shown extending earnestness/earnest care (2Cor 8:16, placing it in Titus's heart), the aspect of divine likeness instantiated is God's own active, purposeful care for his people -- the person's earnestness toward others mirrors God's own earnest care extended toward them.

795.text: Shared between God and the person: 2Cor 8:16 shows God himself placing 'the same earnest care' in Titus that Paul has for the Corinthians -- the identical quality (spoudē) is attributed to both God's giving and the human recipient's possession, not merely an analogue.

797.text: The pattern of occurrence shows the characteristic seated primarily at the level of will/spirit engaged in directed action, paired explicitly with 'spirit' in Rom 12:11 ('fervent in spirit') and with 'heart' in 2Cor 8:16 (placed 'into the heart of Titus'). It never engages purely bodily/sensory levels in isolation, though physical motion (haste, Mark 6:25; Luke 1:39) is its outward expression. The heart/spirit link here is expressive -- the inner earnestness expresses itself outwardly through bodily action (hurrying) or verbal/practical deeds (pleading, providing), rather than the body generating the earnestness itself.

798.text: The body link runs from inner disposition (heart/spirit) outward to bodily action: the earnest care placed in Titus's heart (2Cor 8:16) and the zeal/fervency of spirit (Rom 12:11) express themselves through physical haste (Mark 6:25; Luke 1:39) and active service. There is no instance of bodily feedback generating or intensifying the inner disposition in the reverse direction within this evidence; the direction is consistently spirit/heart-to-body/action.

799.text: Yes, movement is evidenced onto the person from an external source in 2Cor 8:16 -- God places earnest care 'into the heart of Titus', an inward-then-outward sequence (God to heart, heart to action toward the Corinthians). Elsewhere the movement is internally generated (spirit/heart to bodily action) without an external divine source named, as in Rom 12:11's spirit-to-service sequence.

800.text: God's extension of the characteristic in 2Cor 8:16 is unconditional and responsive -- given freely by God ('who put into the heart of Titus') in response to Paul's own existing earnest care for the Corinthians, prompting thanksgiving rather than being earned or conditioned on prior merit by Titus.

801.text: God's giving of earnest care shows a disposition of active, personal involvement in the well-being of his people -- he is not distant but works through his servants' hearts to secure ongoing practical care for the church, evidencing a relational, providential disposition.

802.text: Genuine extension of the characteristic from one person to another accompanies love that is sincere rather than merely commanded (2Cor 8:8, 'not as a command, but to prove... that your love also is genuine') and a heart already shaped by God's own gift of care (2Cor 8:16) -- the giver's inward sincerity and divinely-worked disposition underlie true extension.

803.text: A person must first receive the quality from God (as Titus received earnest care placed in his heart, 2Cor 8:16) before extending it genuinely to others -- the giving is grounded in a prior reception, not self-generated.

807.text: No occurrence in this subgroup shows earnestness/diligence being communicated, strengthened, or mediated through angelic ministry; its extension is shown as coming directly from God to a human heart (2Cor 8:16) without an angelic intermediary.

808.text: The origin is multiple and context-dependent: sometimes internally generated within the person themselves as their own resolve/effort (Luke 7:4's elders, Titus 3:13's imperative, 2Pet 1:5's self-applied effort), and sometimes explicitly God-given (2Cor 8:16, placed by God into Titus's heart). The subgroup shows no single fixed origin -- it shifts between human self-motivation and divine impartation depending on context.

809.text: The characteristic consistently engages the will/volitional faculty (deciding to act with intensity) and frequently the affective faculty (spirit/heart, as in Rom 12:11's 'fervent in spirit' and 2Cor 8:16's 'heart') but never the purely cognitive/reasoning faculty in isolation -- it is not primarily a matter of understanding or belief-formation but of engaged will and feeling directed into action, indicating its nature as a motivational rather than cognitive characteristic.

19678.text: Deuteronomy 23:16 — "in the place that he shall choose … wherever it suits him": The law concerns *"a slave who has escaped from his master to you"*. Israel is told *"You shall not give up to his master"* (v15). Then the choice is handed to the slave: *"He shall dwell with you, in your midst, in the place that he shall choose within one of your towns, wherever it suits him. You shall not wrong him"* (v16).; The man who escaped had no say over where he lived. The law gives it back to him. The choice is his, and its ground is his own good: *"wherever it suits him"* is literally "in what is good to him" (H2896A). Israel's part is to honour it: not to hand him back, and not to *"wrong him"* (H3238, to oppress).; The phrase is a weighty one in Deuteronomy. *"the place that he shall choose within one of your towns"* has the same shape as the phrase Deuteronomy uses for the Lord’s own choosing: *"the place that the Lord your God will choose out of all your tribes"* (12:5); *"the place that the Lord will choose in one of your tribes"* (12:14). The words (place, that, choose, in one of your …) are the same (H4725, H0977). I read this as the law giving the escaped slave, in his own small measure, the kind of choosing the Lord keeps for his own dwelling. The verse does not draw the comparison.
